Positive and negative indexing.syntax: a[i]  ·  a[-1]  # 0-based from the front, -1 from the end
steps: Print `a[-2]` to show the count continues backwards.
Positive and negative indexing.realWorld: Reading the newest record without knowing the row count: `logs[-1]` means "the latest" and survives a growing file.
mistakes: Assuming index 1 is the first element.
Using `-0` (it is just 0).
Indexing past the end and expecting None instead of IndexError.
revision: Indexes are 0-based.
Negative indexes count from the end.

Rows and cells in 2-D.syntax: a[row, column]  ·  a[row]  # cell vs whole row
steps: Print `a[0]` and note the shape is (3,).
Rows and cells in 2-D.realWorld: Reading one measured value from a feature matrix by row (sample) and column (feature) is the most common lookup in data work.
mistakes: Writing `a[0][1]` out of habit — it works but is slower and hides the pair.
Expecting a row index to keep the 2-D shape.
Swapping row and column when the table is transposed.
revision: Row first, column second.
One integer index consumes that axis.

Fancy indexing with an index array.syntax: a[[0, 2]]  # pick positions, in this order
steps: Select positions 0 and 2 with a list.
Select `[2, 0]` and show the order follows the request.
Fancy indexing with an index array.realWorld: Reordering a table by a stored sort order, or sampling specific rows for a report, is one list index away.
mistakes: Assuming the result is sorted — it follows the index order.
Using a list where a slice is meant, which copies instead of viewing.
Passing floats or booleans by accident and getting mask semantics.
revision: Fancy indexing returns a copy in the requested order.
Duplicates and repeats are allowed.

steps: Print its type to show it is a NumPy scalar, not an array.
Index with a coordinate pair.realWorld: Pulling a single metric out of a results grid — one number for a headline — is a coordinate lookup, not a slice.
mistakes: Using two brackets `a[1][2]` and losing the vectorised intent.
Expecting a 0-d array and getting a scalar (or vice versa).
Forgetting that the pair is (row, column), not (x, y).
revision: Two indices inside one bracket address one cell.
The result is a scalar.

steps: Keep the axis with `a[0:1]` and print its shape.
One index drops a dimension.realWorld: Broadcasting a row against a column fails because the row lost its axis; keeping the dimension with a slice fixes the shape.
mistakes: Treating a 1-D row as a (1, n) row vector.
Adding `.reshape` everywhere instead of using a slice.
Assuming shape (3,) and (1, 3) print the same way (they do not).
revision: Integer indexing removes the axis.
Slicing keeps it.

steps: Print `a[:, 1].shape` and compare with the matrix.
Select a whole column.realWorld: One feature column across all samples is exactly this expression, and it is the input to most per-feature statistics.
mistakes: Writing `a[1]` and getting a row instead of a column.
Expecting a (2, 1) result from an integer column index.
Mutating the column and forgetting it is a view.
revision: Colon keeps the row axis.
An integer column index drops the column axis.

steps: Print the shape to show three rows came back.
Fancy indexing picks rows.realWorld: Bootstrapping a sample by repeating rows, or duplicating a header row for a report, needs repeated indices — a slice cannot do it.
mistakes: Expecting fancy indexing to return a view.
Assuming repeated indices are deduplicated.
Mixing a list of rows with a single column index without a comma.
revision: A list of row indices returns rows in that order.
Repeats are preserved and the result is a copy.

steps: Compare with the equivalent bracket expression.
take works along an axis.realWorld: Named-axis selection reads better in a pipeline: `take(..., axis=1)` says "columns" without the reader decoding a colon.
mistakes: Forgetting `axis` and flattening the array by default.
Assuming `take` returns a view.
Mixing axis 0 and axis 1 when the table is wide.
revision: `take` names the axis explicitly.
Default axis is the flattened array.

steps: Apply the same idea to a row of a matrix.
Negative indices count from the end.realWorld: Grabbing the most recent measurement works regardless of how many rows the file grew to.
mistakes: Using `a[len(a)]` instead of `a[-1]`.
Assuming `-1` means "before the first".
Forgetting the same rule works per axis in 2-D.
revision: `-1` is the last element.
The rule applies on every axis.

Slice columns of a matrix.realWorld: Feature selection before a model is a column slice; keeping it a slice preserves the 2-D shape the model expects.
mistakes: Losing the second axis by using an integer instead of a slice.
Assuming `a[:, 0:1]` is the same shape as `a[:, 0]`.
Mutating the slice and being surprised the matrix changed.
revision: Slice columns with `:, start:stop`.
A slice keeps the column axis.

A boolean mask filters one dimension.syntax: a[a > 5]  # mask must match the shape
steps: Build the mask `a > 5` and print it.
Index with the mask and print the kept values.
A boolean mask filters one dimension.realWorld: Filtering a column by a business rule — orders above a threshold — is one comparison and one index, with no loop.
mistakes: Using `and`/`or` between comparisons instead of `&`/`|`.
Passing a mask of the wrong length.
Expecting the mask to change the original array.
revision: Masks are boolean arrays of the same shape.
Filtering copies the kept values.

steps: Print the result and explain it is (0,1) and (2,2).
Index with paired row and column lists.realWorld: Reading a diagonal or a set of specific (row, column) measurements — paired indexing is the precise tool.
mistakes: Expecting a 2×2 crossing of the two lists.
Using a slice for one of the two lists by accident.
Mismatched list lengths, which raises.
revision: Two index arrays are zipped element by element.
The result has the length of the index arrays.

steps: Print the row, the column and one cell.
Rows, columns and single cells.realWorld: A data inspection notebook moves between these three constantly; knowing which one keeps which axis prevents most shape bugs.
mistakes: Using a colon where an integer was meant, or vice versa.
Assuming all three return the same shape.
Forgetting that a cell is a scalar, not a length-1 array.
revision: Integer = one item, colon = all items.
Row and column are 1-D; a cell is scalar.

steps: Add an axis to a vector with `np.newaxis` and print the shape.
Ellipsis and newaxis.realWorld: Keeping code readable for n-dimensional tensors: `...` avoids counting colons, and `newaxis` is how a vector becomes a row for broadcasting.
mistakes: Using `...` when an explicit axis would be clearer.
Confusing `np.newaxis` with `np.expand_dims` (same result, different spelling).
Adding an axis at the wrong position and broadcasting along the wrong dimension.
revision: `...` stands for all unnamed axes.
`np.newaxis` inserts a length-1 axis.
